description: How America's open door slammed shut: the Palmer Raids, immigration acts and Sacco and Vanzetti.
content_html:
The Open Door: Immigration Before 1920

In the decades before the First World War, the United States operated what was often called an open door policy on immigration. Between 1880 and 1914, approximately 20 million people arrived in the United States, many of them coming through Ellis Island in New York harbour. The majority came from southern and eastern Europe — Italians, Poles, Russians and Jews fleeing poverty or persecution. Many settled in crowded urban neighbourhoods, taking low-paid factory work. By 1910, over a third of the United States’ population was either foreign-born or the children of immigrants.

Not everyone welcomed this wave of newcomers. Many native-born Americans feared economic competition for jobs and wages. Some held deeply racist beliefs, arguing that immigrants from southern and eastern Europe were racially inferior to those from northern and western Europe. These views fed a growing demand for restrictions on immigration.

Key Fact

Between 1880 and 1914, roughly 20 million immigrants entered the United States. The majority came from southern and eastern Europe, and many passed through Ellis Island. This huge influx fuelled a nativist backlash that eventually produced major immigration restrictions in the 1920s.

Restricting Immigration: The Acts of 1921 and 1924

Congress responded to anti-immigration pressure with two landmark laws. The Emergency Quota Act of 1921 introduced national origin quotas for the first time, capping each nationality’s annual intake at 3 per cent of that nationality’s population already in America as recorded in the 1910 census. This reduced total immigration to around 357,000 per year — a sharp drop from the pre-war peak of over a million annually.

Three years later, the Immigration Act of 1924 tightened restrictions further. It cut the quota to 2 per cent of each nationality’s 1890 census figure — a deliberate choice, because far fewer southern and eastern Europeans lived in America in 1890. The act also set an annual cap of 164,667 immigrants and imposed a near-total ban on Asian immigration. The practical effect was to favour immigration from Britain, Germany and Scandinavia while drastically limiting arrivals from Italy, Poland and Russia.

Behind the quota system lay nativism — a fear that immigrants were changing the character of the United States. Influential works such as Madison Grant’s The Passing of the Great Race (1916) argued, using pseudo-scientific racial theory, that immigration from southern and eastern Europe would lead to racial and cultural decline. Such ideas had a real influence on legislators and public opinion during the 1920s.

Economic anxieties also played a role. After the First World War, many returning soldiers found that immigrants had taken their factory jobs. Trade unions, particularly the American Federation of Labor, lobbied for restrictions to protect wage levels. The combination of racial prejudice and economic competition made immigration restriction broadly popular across American society.

The Red Scare, 1919–1920

The end of the First World War brought a new fear to the United States: communism. The Bolshevik Revolution in Russia in 1917 had brought a communist government to power, and in 1919, a wave of strikes and bomb attacks across American cities stoked alarm that a similar revolution was being plotted at home. This period of panic became known as the First Red Scare.

In April 1919, postal workers intercepted packages containing letter bombs addressed to prominent politicians and businessmen. In June, simultaneous bombings in eight cities targeted government officials. Although the perpetrators were never fully identified, the attacks were widely blamed on anarchist and communist immigrants. Fear of foreign-born radicals merged with the existing anti-immigration mood.

Key Fact

The Palmer Raids of November 1919 and January 1920, led by Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer, resulted in the arrest of approximately 10,000 suspected radicals across 33 cities. Hundreds were deported without trial. The raids alarmed civil liberties groups and were later criticised as unlawful.

The Palmer Raids

Attorney General A. Mitchell Palmer responded to the bombing campaign by launching a series of raids on suspected radical organisations. The Palmer Raids took place in November 1919 and on the night of 2–3 January 1920. In the January raid alone, agents arrested approximately 3,000 people in 33 cities in a single night. Many were held without charge; some were deported without trial. The most prominent deportee was the anarchist Emma Goldman, who was sent to Russia in December 1919.

The raids were eventually condemned by legal experts and civil liberties groups. In May 1920, a group of twelve eminent lawyers published a report describing them as a systematic violation of constitutional rights. Palmer’s credibility collapsed when his predicted uprising on 1 May 1920 failed to materialise. The raids were significant, however, in linking immigration, radicalism and foreignness in the public mind — a connection that shaped the immigration restrictions of the 1920s.

In April 1920, a paymaster and a security guard were murdered during a robbery at a shoe factory in South Braintree, Massachusetts. Two Italian-born anarchists, Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti, were arrested and charged with the murders. Both men denied the charges but were convicted in July 1921 after a trial widely criticised for bias: witnesses who provided alibis were dismissed, and the judge made prejudicial remarks about the defendants’ anarchist beliefs and foreign origins.

The case became an international cause. Protests were held across Europe and Latin America. Intellectuals and writers condemned the trial as a miscarriage of justice rooted in anti-immigrant prejudice and anti-anarchist hysteria. After several appeals failed, Sacco and Vanzetti were executed on 23 August 1927. Their case remains the most famous symbol of American nativism and the dangers of political prejudice in the justice system during the 1920s. Massachusetts officially acknowledged in 1977 that they had not received a fair trial.

The United States as a Nation of Contrasts

The immigration restrictions of the 1920s reveal one of the deepest contradictions in American life. The United States had built its wealth and identity on immigration, yet it moved decisively to close the door — driven by racial prejudice, economic anxiety and political fear. For millions of would-be immigrants, the American dream became inaccessible. For those who were already there, the Red Scare and the Sacco and Vanzetti case showed how quickly rights could be stripped away when fear and prejudice dominated public life.
exam_tip_html: When answering a “5 marks — Source Utility” question on immigration or the Red Scare, always combine three things: what the source says (content), who produced it and why (provenance), and what you know from your own knowledge that confirms or challenges it (contextual knowledge). Mentioning only provenance (“it is biased because Palmer had a reason to exaggerate”) will only reach the lower marks. For 8-mark or 12-mark questions on the significance or consequences of the immigration acts, make sure to address both the immediate impact (numbers deported, quotas set) and the longer-term significance (the message sent to minority communities, the closing of the open door).
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Between 1880 and 1914, around 20 million immigrants entered the United States through Ellis Island, mostly from southern and eastern Europe. Growing nativist and economic fears produced the Emergency Quota Act (1921) and the Immigration Act (1924), which severely restricted immigration from southern and eastern Europe.
  • The Red Scare of 1919–1920 linked immigration with communism and anarchism in the public mind. The Palmer Raids arrested approximately 10,000 people; hundreds were deported without trial. The scare reflected deep tensions between civil liberties and national security fears.
  • The Sacco and Vanzetti case (1920–1927) became the defining symbol of anti-immigrant prejudice in the justice system. Both men were executed in 1927 despite widespread international protest, and Massachusetts later acknowledged they had not received a fair trial.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Emergency Quota Act of 1921.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for identifying a feature; one mark for supporting detail.
Example: The Emergency Quota Act introduced national origin quotas [1], capping annual immigration of each nationality at 3 per cent of that nationality's population in America as recorded by the 1910 census [1].
Other acceptable features: it reduced annual immigration to approximately 357,000; it was the first time the US government had used a quota system for immigration.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Palmer Raids.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks per feature: one for the feature, one for supporting detail.
Feature 1: The Palmer Raids arrested large numbers of suspected radicals — approximately 10,000 people across 33 cities, many detained without warrants. [2]
Feature 2: Those arrested were frequently deported without trial — the most prominent deportee was the anarchist Emma Goldman, sent to Russia in December 1919. [2]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of the growing demand for immigration restrictions in the United States after the First World War.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains a specific cause with precise factual support and clear causal reasoning, addressing both the cause and its link to the outcome.
Secure: Identifies a valid cause with some supporting evidence and a clear explanatory link.
Developing: Names a cause but explanation is limited or generic.
Emerging: Simple statement with little development.
Valid causes: nativist racial ideology (e.g. Madison Grant); economic competition for jobs after the war; fear of communism and anarchism linking immigrants to radicalism; the Red Scare linking foreignness to political threat.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the Red Scare for immigrants living in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Traces a consequence with precise evidence and clear reasoning about how the Red Scare produced that outcome.
Secure: Identifies a valid consequence with supporting detail.
Developing: Names a consequence but the causal link is vague.
Emerging: Simple point.
Valid consequences: thousands of immigrants arrested and deported without trial during the Palmer Raids; immigrants associated with radicalism regardless of individual beliefs; increased public support for immigration restriction laws; climate of fear for immigrant communities.

practice_questions.text:
How significant was the Sacco and Vanzetti case in revealing the treatment of immigrants in the United States in the 1920s?
Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses significance both at the time and in the longer term, with precise evidence and sustained analysis.
Secure: Explains significance with relevant detail; may address only one timeframe fully.
Developing: Some explanation of significance but limited evidence.
Emerging: Simple points.
At the time: exposed racial and political prejudice in the justice system; provoked international protests; made immigrants afraid; discredited anti-immigrant hysteria.
Over time: became a symbol of nativism; Massachusetts acknowledged in 1977 that they had not received a fair trial; shaped later debates about justice and immigration.

practice_questions.text:
'The Immigration Act of 1924 was the most important turning point in US immigration policy in the years 1910 to 1929.'
How far do you agree with this interpretation? Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Agrees and disagrees with specific evidence for both positions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.
Secure: Makes points for and against with relevant evidence; judgement present but may be underdeveloped.
Developing: Some relevant points but response is unbalanced or lacks a clear judgement.
Emerging: Simple agreement or disagreement with limited support.
Agreement: The 1924 act introduced the most restrictive quotas using the 1890 baseline, effectively ended mass immigration from southern and eastern Europe, imposed near-total Asian exclusion, and set the template for US immigration policy until 1965.
Disagreement: The 1921 Quota Act introduced the quota principle first; the Red Scare and Palmer Raids shaped anti-immigrant attitudes before either act; Sacco and Vanzetti showed that prejudice already existed in the system.

knowledge_checks.q: Which law, passed in 1921, first introduced national origin quotas for immigration to the United States?
Who led the government raids in 1919-1920 that arrested thousands of suspected radicals, many of them immigrants?
Nicola Sacco and Bartolomeo Vanzetti were Italian-born _____ who were convicted of murder in 1921 after a widely criticised trial.
The Immigration Act of 1924 used the _____ census as its baseline for calculating national quotas, deliberately reducing immigration from southern and eastern Europe.
Match each term to its correct description:
right: The belief that America should be reserved for native-born white Protestants
A period of anti-communist panic in the United States in 1919-1920
An immigration processing station in New York harbour

flashcard_questions.q: When was Ellis Island opened as the main US immigration processing station?
Approximately how many immigrants entered the United States between 1880 and 1914?
What did the Emergency Quota Act of 1921 set as the annual immigration limit for each nationality?
flashcard_questions.a: 3 per cent of that nationality's US population in the 1910 census.

flashcard_questions.q: Which census year did the Immigration Act of 1924 use as its baseline, and why was this significant?
flashcard_questions.a: 1890 — far fewer southern and eastern Europeans lived in America then, so their quotas were tiny.

flashcard_questions.q: The period of anti-communist panic in America in 1919-1920 is known as the ___.
Who was Attorney General during the Palmer Raids of 1919-1920?
Approximately how many people were arrested in the January 1920 Palmer Raid across 33 cities?
Which prominent anarchist was deported to Russia in December 1919 following the Palmer Raids?
What crime were Sacco and Vanzetti convicted of in July 1921?
flashcard_questions.a: Murder during a payroll robbery in South Braintree, Massachusetts.

flashcard_questions.q: When were Sacco and Vanzetti executed?
What did Massachusetts officially acknowledge in 1977 regarding Sacco and Vanzetti?
flashcard_questions.a: That they had not received a fair trial.

flashcard_questions.q: What book by Madison Grant (1916) gave pseudo-scientific support to nativist immigration restriction?
flashcard_questions.a: The Passing of the Great Race.

glossary_terms.definition: The policy, common before the 1920s, of allowing immigrants to enter the United States with few restrictions.
An immigration processing station on an island in New York harbour, through which over 12 million immigrants passed between 1892 and 1954.
A law passed in 1921 that set annual immigration quotas based on the number of each nationality already living in the United States in 1910, limiting total immigration to about 357,000 per year.
The belief that America should be reserved for its native-born white Protestant population, and that immigration threatened American culture and identity.
A period of intense anti-communist fear and suspicion in the United States in 1919-1920, during which thousands of suspected radicals were arrested and deported.
Government operations in 1919-1920 in which federal agents arrested thousands of suspected anarchists and communists, many of them immigrants, often without warrants.
